llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: This 11-year-old female presents with clinical features consistent with two concurrent diagnoses: Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) - The classic "slapped cheek" appearance with reddened cheeks, combined with the red, lacy rash on bilateral upper extremities (wrists to elbows) and faint involvement of the lower back, is pathognomonic for parvovirus B19 infection. The pruritic nature of the rash and known outbreak at school further support this diagnosis. The patient is presenting during the rash phase, which corresponds to the immune-mediated stage of infection when she is no longer contagious. Acute bacterial sinusitis - The patient meets clinical criteria for acute bacterial sinusitis with purulent nasal discharge, bilateral maxillary sinus tenderness, left frontal sinus tenderness, postnasal drainage, and symptoms including facial pressure/headache and sore throat. The swollen, red nasal mucosa with purulent discharge in the posterior turbinates on examination supports bacterial rather than viral etiology. The patient's asthma is currently well-controlled with clear lung fields and no wheezing. PLAN: Fifth disease (erythema infectiosum): Continue symptomatic management with diphenhydramine as needed for pruritus Reassurance that the rash is self-limited and will resolve spontaneously Educate family that the rash may wax and wane with triggers such as sunlight, heat, exercise, or emotional stress Patient is no longer contagious once rash appears No specific antiviral treatment indicated Acute bacterial sinusitis: Amoxicillin 500 mg orally twice daily for 10 days (weight-based dosing: approximately 45 mg/kg/day divided twice daily) Supportive care: saline nasal irrigation, adequate hydration, analgesics as needed for facial pain/headache May continue diphenhydramine for symptomatic relief if needed Asthma: No treatment needed at this time given current stability Continue to monitor for any respiratory symptoms Follow-up: Return to clinic or call if sinusitis symptoms worsen or fail to improve within 3-5 days of starting antibiotics Return if rash becomes painful, develops purpura, or if new symptoms develop Routine follow-up as needed
llm_dx_summary: An 11-year-old female presents with classic signs of erythema infectiosum characterized by a 'slapped cheek' rash and a red, lacy rash on the extremities, along with clinical features consistent with acute bacterial sinusitis including purulent nasal discharge and sinus tenderness.

presentation: SUBJECTIVE:,  This is a followup dietary consultation for hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and possible metabolic syndrome.  The patient reports that she has worked hard for a number of weeks following the meal plan prescribed, but felt like she was gaining weight and not losing weight on it.  She is not sure that she was following it accurately.  She is trying to walk 1-1/2 to 2 miles every other day, but is increasing her time in the garden and doing other yard work as well.  Once she started experiencing some weight gain, she went back to her old South Beach Diet and felt like she was able to take some of that weight off.  However she realizes that the South Beach Diet is not a healthy diet for her and so is coming back for better instruction on safe weight loss and low-fat eating.,OBJECTIVE:,  Weight is 275 pounds.  Food records were reviewed.,
human_ap: ASSESSMENT:,  The patient experienced a weight gain of 2 pounds since our last consultation which was two months ago.  I did carefully review her food records and evaluated calories consumed.  While she was carefully tracking the volume of protein and carbohydrates, she was getting some excess calories from the fatty proteins selected.  Thus we rearranged her meal plan a little bit and talked about how to track her fat calories as well.  She was more open to reducing the amount of protein from the previous meal plan and increasing slightly the amount of carbohydrates.  While this still is not as much carbohydrate as I would normally recommend, I am certainly willing to work with her on how she feels her body best handles weight reduction.  We also discussed a snack that could be eliminated in the morning because she really is not hungry at that time.,PLAN:,  A new 1500 calorie meal plan was developed based on 35% of the calories coming from protein, 40% of the calories from carbohydrate, and 25% of the calories from fat.  This translates in to 10 servings at 15 grams a piece of carbohydrates throughout the day dividing them in to groups of two servings per meal and per snack.  This also translates in to 2 ounces of protein at breakfast, 6 ounces at lunch, 2 ounces in the afternoon snack, 6 ounces at supper, and 2 ounces in the evening snack.  We have eliminated the morning snack.  The patient will now track the grams of fat in her meats as well as added fats.  Her goal for total fats over the course of the day is no more than 42 grams of fat per day.  This was a half hour consultation.  We will plan to see the patient back in one month for support.

Excess calorie intake from fatty proteins

llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: This 275-pound patient presents for follow-up dietary consultation with hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and possible metabolic syndrome. The patient reports difficulty adhering to the prescribed meal plan, with perceived weight gain rather than loss. She subsequently returned to the South Beach Diet with subjective improvement but recognizes this is not optimal for her cardiovascular risk factors. She is engaging in regular physical activity (walking 1.5-2 miles every other day plus gardening/yard work), which is commendable. PLAN: Dietary Intervention: Transition to Mediterranean or DASH dietary pattern, which have the strongest evidence for cardiovascular risk reduction Emphasize: high intake of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, fish; moderate olive oil use; low saturated fat, minimal red meat, limited added sugars and refined carbohydrates Target caloric deficit of 500-750 kcal/day to achieve gradual weight loss Specific recommendations: limit saturated fat, avoid trans fats, minimize alcohol, reduce sodium intake to 1500 mg/day for blood pressure control Weight Loss Goals: Target 5-10% body weight reduction over 6 months (approximately 14-27 pounds) Weekly weight loss goal: 1-2 pounds per week through combination of dietary modification and physical activity Physical Activity: Continue current walking regimen (1.5-2 miles every other day) and yard work Goal: progress toward 150-225 minutes/week of moderate-intensity aerobic activity for sustained weight loss Add resistance exercise 2 days/week Laboratory Testing: Fasting lipid panel (total cholesterol, LDL-C, HDL-C, triglycerides, non-HDL-C) Fasting glucose and hemoglobin A1c to assess for diabetes/prediabetes Basic metabolic panel Consider apolipoprotein B if available Referral: Formal consultation with registered dietitian nutritionist (RDN) for individualized meal planning, portion control education, and ongoing dietary counseling Pharmacotherapy Consideration: If lifestyle modifications do not achieve adequate weight loss after 3-6 months, consider obesity pharmacotherapy (e.g., GLP-1 receptor agonists, GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists, or naltrexone/bupropion) given BMI and cardiovascular risk factors Optimize antihypertensive and lipid-lowering medications as indicated by laboratory results Follow-up: Return visit in 4-6 weeks to review laboratory results, assess dietary adherence, monitor weight loss progress, and adjust plan as needed Monthly follow-up thereafter for first 6 months Monitor blood pressure at each visit

presentation: SUBJECTIVE:,  This is a 38-year-old female who comes for dietary consultation for gestational diabetes.  Patient reports that she is scared to eat because of its impact on her blood sugars.  She is actually trying not to eat while she is working third shift at Wal-Mart.  Historically however, she likes to eat out with a high frequency.  She enjoys eating rice as part of her meals.  She is complaining of feeling fatigued and tired all the time because she works from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m. at Wal-Mart and has young children at home.  She sleeps two to four hours at a time throughout the day.  She has been testing for ketones first thing in the morning when she gets home from work.,OBJECTIVE:,  Today's weight:  155.5 pounds.  Weight from 10/07/04 was 156.7 pounds.  A diet history was obtained.  Blood sugar records for the last three days reveal the following:  fasting blood sugars 83, 84, 87, 77; two-hour postprandial breakfast 116, 107, 97; pre-lunch 85, 108, 77; two-hour postprandial lunch 86, 131, 100; pre-supper 78, 91, 100; two-hour postprandial supper 125, 121, 161; bedtime 104, 90 and 88.  I instructed the patient on dietary guidelines for gestational diabetes.  The Lily Guide for Meal Planning was provided and reviewed.  Additional information on gestational diabetes was applied.  A sample 2000-calorie meal plan was provided with a carbohydrate budget established.,
human_ap: ASSESSMENT:,  Patient's basal energy expenditure adjusted for obesity is estimated at 1336 calories a day.  Her total calorie requirements, including a physical activity factor as well as additional calories for pregnancy, totals to 2036 calories per day.  Her diet history reveals that she has somewhat irregular eating patterns.  In the last 24 hours when she was working at Wal-Mart, she ate at 5 a.m. but did not eat anything prior to that since starting work at 10 p.m.  We discussed the need for small frequent eating.  We identified carbohydrate as the food source that contributes to the blood glucose response.  We identified carbohydrate sources in the food supply, recognizing that they are all good for her.  The only carbohydrates she was asked to entirely avoid would be the concentrated forms of refined sugars.  In regard to use of her traditional foods of rice, I pulled out a one-third cup measuring cup to identify a 15-gram equivalent of rice.  We discussed the need for moderating the portion of carbohydrates consumed at one given time.  Emphasis was placed at eating with a high frequency with a goal of eating every two to four hours over the course of the day when she is awake.  Her weight loss was discouraged.  Patient was encouraged to eat more generously but with attention to the amount of carbohydrates consumed at a time.,PLAN:,  The meal plan provided has a carbohydrate content that represents 40 percent of a 2000-calorie meal plan.  The meal plan was devised to distribute her carbohydrates more evenly throughout the day.  The meal plan was meant to reflect an example for her eating, while the patient was encouraged to eat according to appetite and not to go without eating for long periods of time.  The meal plan is as follows:  breakfast 2 carbohydrate servings, snack 1 carbohydrate serving, lunch 2-3 carbohydrate servings, snack 1 carbohydrate serving, dinner 2-3 carbohydrate servings, bedtime snack 1-2 carbohydrate servings.  Recommend patient include a solid protein with each of her meals as well as with her snack that occurs before going to sleep.  Encouraged adequate rest.  Also recommend adequate calories to sustain weight gain of one-half to one pound per week.  If the meal plan reflected does not support slow gradual weight gain, then we will need to add more foods accordingly.  This was a one-hour consultation.  I provided my name and number should additional needs arise.

llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), well-controlled with medical nutrition therapy This 38-year-old pregnant female with GDM demonstrates excellent glycemic control on her current dietary regimen. Her blood glucose values over the past three days are consistently within target ranges: fasting values 77-87 mg/dL (target <95 mg/dL), and 2-hour postprandial values 86-161 mg/dL (target <120 mg/dL). Only one value (161 mg/dL post-supper) exceeded target in the past three days, representing <5% of measurements. However, there is significant concern for inadequate caloric and carbohydrate intake with resultant starvation ketosis. The patient reports fear of eating and actively restricting food intake while working overnight shifts. She is checking for morning ketonuria, which suggests awareness of potential ketosis. Her weight has decreased 1.2 pounds over approximately one month. The combination of ketonuria, weight loss, fatigue, and food restriction raises concern for insufficient caloric intake, which can lead to maternal ketosis and potentially adverse fetal outcomes. Pregnant women require a minimum of 175 g of carbohydrate daily to prevent starvation ketosis. The patient's challenging work schedule (overnight shifts 10 PM-7 AM) with minimal sleep (2-4 hours fragmented throughout the day) and young children at home creates significant barriers to adequate nutrition and self-care. PLAN: Nutrition counseling reinforcement: Emphasize that the 2,000-calorie meal plan with adequate carbohydrate intake (minimum 175 g/day) is essential for both maternal and fetal health Reassure patient that her blood glucose control is excellent and she should not fear eating appropriate portions Address misconception that restricting food intake is beneficial; explain risks of inadequate carbohydrate intake including ketosis Provide practical strategies for eating during overnight shifts, including portable meal options and scheduled eating times Recommend complex carbohydrates with low glycemic index to maintain stable glucose levels Ketone monitoring: Continue daily first morning urine ketone testing Instruct patient to contact clinic immediately if ketones are moderate or large, or if she experiences nausea, vomiting, or inability to eat If persistent ketonuria despite adequate reported intake, consider checking serum beta-hydroxybutyrate for more accurate assessment Glucose monitoring: Continue current regimen: fasting and 2-hour postprandial testing after each meal (4 times daily) No pharmacologic therapy indicated at this time given excellent glycemic control Threshold for initiating insulin would be >20% of values above target or >5 abnormal values in 7 days Follow-up: Return visit in 1 week to review glucose logs, ketone results, food diary, and weight Consider referral to social work or case management to address work-life balance challenges Continue weekly visits with review of glucose and ketone logs Patient education: Reinforce that well-controlled GDM with adequate nutrition has excellent pregnancy outcomes Provide written materials on safe eating during overnight work shifts Encourage adequate hydration and rest when possible

Inadequate caloric and carbohydrate intake with resultant starvation ketosis

She walks her daughter to school and back home each day which takes 20 minutes each way.  She is not a big milk drinker, but she does try to drink some.,OBJECTIVE:,  Weight is 238.3 pounds.  Weight from last week’s visit was 238.9 pounds.  Prepregnancy weight is reported at 235 pounds.  Height is 62-3/4 inches.  Prepregnancy BMI is approximately 42-1/2. human_ap: ASSESSMENT:,  Patient’s basal energy expenditure adjusted for obesity is estimated at 1566 calories a day.  Her total calorie requirements, including physical activity factors as well as additional calories for pregnancy, totals 2367 calories a day. llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: Recurrent hypoglycemia in insulin-treated diabetes with paradoxically decreasing insulin requirements. Despite substantial reduction in insulin doses (Lantus from 84 units to 60 units, with corresponding decreases in Humalog), the patient continues to experience morning hypoglycemia (glucose in 70s) without compensatory hyperglycemia. This pattern is atypical and concerning. The patient maintains good appetite and oral intake per staff report. The differential diagnosis for unexplained decreasing insulin requirements includes: Hypoglycemia-associated autonomic failure (HAAF) with recurrent nocturnal hypoglycemia Improved insulin sensitivity from unrecognized factors Development of adrenal insufficiency or other endocrinopathy Progression of chronic kidney disease with decreased insulin clearance Unrecognized medication changes or interactions Occult malignancy (non-islet cell tumor hypoglycemia) The patient's fatigue may represent either hypoglycemia symptoms or an underlying systemic process. PLAN: Insulin adjustment: Further reduce Lantus to 50 units at bedtime Continue to reduce Humalog sliding scale doses proportionally Consider splitting basal insulin to twice daily if morning hypoglycemia persists Temporarily relax glycemic targets to avoid hypoglycemia Enhanced glucose monitoring: Implement continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) if available to identify nocturnal hypoglycemia patterns If CGM unavailable, increase frequency of bedside glucose monitoring to include 3 AM checks for 3-5 nights Document all hypoglycemic episodes with timing, symptoms, and treatment Laboratory evaluation to identify underlying causes: Comprehensive metabolic panel (assess renal function, electrolytes) Hemoglobin A1C (assess overall glycemic control) TSH, free T4 (screen for hypothyroidism) Morning cortisol (8 AM) or ACTH stimulation test if morning cortisol low (screen for adrenal insufficiency) Complete blood count (assess for anemia, systemic illness) Liver function tests (assess hepatic function affecting insulin clearance) Medication review: Comprehensive review of all medications for potential drug interactions or recent changes Verify insulin types, concentrations, and administration technique with nursing staff Nutritional assessment: Formal dietary consultation to verify caloric intake and meal timing Review recent weight trends Follow-up: Daily reassessment of glucose patterns and insulin requirements Endocrinology consultation if hypoglycemia persists despite further insulin reduction or if laboratory evaluation reveals endocrinopathy Patient/staff education: Educate on hypoglycemia recognition and treatment Ensure glucagon is available at bedside Instruct staff to treat glucose <70 mg/dL with 15 grams fast-acting carbohydrate

llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: Right upper lobe non-small cell lung cancer, stage IA, status post CyberKnife (SABR) completed one month ago. The patient is presenting for her first post-treatment follow-up visit. She reports low-level nausea, pleuritic chest pain with deep inspiration, and resolving dysphagia - all consistent with expected low-grade post-SABR toxicity. Nausea may be related to radiation effect on adjacent structures or concurrent medications. Pleuritic pain is a recognized side effect of thoracic SBRT, particularly when the tumor is in proximity to the chest wall. Resolving dysphagia suggests mild esophageal irritation from treatment. She denies cough, hemoptysis, rash, or palpable rib pain, and her lungs are clear to auscultation, making clinically significant radiation pneumonitis unlikely at this time. Multiple chronic comorbidities including seizure disorder, hypothyroidism, COPD, depression, and chronic pain syndrome. PLAN: Post-SABR surveillance and symptom management: Obtain chest CT with contrast at approximately 3 months post-treatment (i.e., in approximately 2 months) per NCCN surveillance guidelines Thereafter, chest CT every 3-6 months for 3 years, then every 6 months for 2 years, then annual low-dose CT FDG-PET/CT is not routinely indicated for surveillance Smoking cessation counseling reinforced Nausea: Continue omeprazole 20 mg daily May trial ondansetron 4 mg PO q8h PRN for persistent nausea Reassess at next visit Pleuritic chest pain: Continue current analgesic regimen Monitor for worsening pain, which could indicate rib fracture - a known late complication of thoracic SBRT If pain worsens or localizes, obtain dedicated chest wall imaging Resolving dysphagia: Continue omeprazole If dysphagia worsens or fails to resolve within the next 2-4 weeks, consider upper endoscopy Medication concerns: Note that the patient is on two NSAIDs concurrently (naproxen 375 mg BID and oxaprozin 600 mg BID) in addition to Tylenol with Codeine. This carries significant risk for GI bleeding and renal injury. Recommend discontinuing one NSAID and consolidating pain management. Discuss with patient and consider pain management referral if chronic pain is difficult to control. Continue all other medications as prescribed. Follow-up: Return to clinic in 2 months for symptom reassessment and to coordinate first surveillance chest CT at 3 months post-treatment. Sooner if symptoms worsen, including new or worsening dyspnea, hemoptysis, increasing chest pain, or fever.

presentation: CHIEF COMPLAINT:  ,Hip pain.,HISTORY OF PRESENTING ILLNESS:  ,The patient is a very pleasant 41-year-old white female that is known to me previously from our work at the Pain Management Clinic, as well as from my residency training program, San Francisco. We have worked collaboratively for many years at the Pain Management Clinic and with her departure there, she has asked to establish with me for clinic pain management at my office.  She reports moderate to severe pain related to a complicated past medical history.  In essence, she was seen at a very young age at the clinic for bilateral knee and hip pain and diagnosed with bursitis at age 23.  She was given nonsteroidals at that time, which did help with this discomfort.  With time, however, this became inadequate and she was seen later in San Francisco in her mid 30s by Dr. V, an orthopedist who diagnosed retroverted hips at Hospital.  She was referred for rehabilitation and strengthening.  Most of this was focused on her SI joints.  At that time, although she had complained of foot discomfort, she was not treated for it.  This was in 1993 after which she and her new husband moved to the Boston area, where she lived from 1995-1996.  She was seen at the Pain Center by Dr. R with similar complaints of hip and knee pain.  She was seen by rheumatologists there and diagnosed with osteoarthritis as well as osteophytosis of the back.  Medications at that time were salicylate and Ultram.,When she returned to Portland in 1996, she was then working for Dr. B.  She was referred to a podiatrist by her local doctor who found several fractured sesamoid bones in her both feet, but this was later found not to be the case.  Subsequently, nuclear bone scans revealed osteoarthritis.  Orthotics were provided.  She was given Paxil and Tramadol and subsequently developed an unfortunate side effect of grand mal seizure.  During this workup of her seizure, imaging studies revealed a pericardial fluid-filled cyst adhered to her ventricle.  She has been advised not to undergo any corrective or reparative surgery as well as to limit her activities since.  She currently does not have an established cardiologist having just changed insurance plans.  She is establishing care with Dr. S, of Rheumatology for her ongoing care.  Up until today, her pain medications were being written by Dr. Y prior to establishing with Dr. L.,Pain management in town had been first provided by the office of Dr. F. Under his care, followup MRIs were done which showed ongoing degenerative disc disease, joint disease, and facet arthropathy in addition to previously described sacroiliitis.  A number of medications were attempted there, including fentanyl patches with Flonase from 25 mcg titrated upwards to 50 mcg, but this caused oversedation.  She then transferred her care to Ab Cd, FNP under the direction of Dr. K.  Her care there was satisfactory, but because of her work schedule, the patient found this burdensome as well as the guidelines set forth in terms of monthly meetings and routine urine screens.  Because of a previous commitment, she was unable to make one unscheduled request to their office in order to produce a random urine screen and was therefore discharged.,PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:  ,1.  Attention deficit disorder.,2.  TMJ arthropathy.,3.  Migraines.,4.  Osteoarthritis as described above.,PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:,1.  Cystectomies.,2.  Sinuses.,3.  Left ganglia of the head and subdermally in various locations.,4.  TMJ and bruxism.,FAMILY HISTORY:  ,The patient's father also suffered from bilateral hip osteoarthritis.,MEDICATIONS:,1.  Methadone 2.5 mg p.o. t.i.d.,2.  Norco 10/325 mg p.o. q.i.d.,3.  Tenormin 50 mg q.a.m.,4.  Skelaxin 800 mg b.i.d. to t.i.d. p.r.n.,5.  Wellbutrin SR 100 mg q.d.,6.  Naprosyn 500 mg one to two pills q.d. p.r.n.,ALLERGIES: , IV morphine causes hives.  Sulfa caused blisters and rash.,PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: , A well-developed, well-nourished white female in no acute distress, sitting comfortably and answering questions appropriately, making good eye contact, and no evidence of pain behavior.,VITAL SIGNS:  Blood pressure 110/72 with a pulse of 68.,HEENT:  Normocephalic.  Atraumatic.  Pupils are equal and reactive to light and accommodation.  Extraocular motions are intact.  No scleral icterus.  No nystagmus.  Tongue is midline.  Mucous membranes are moist without exudate.,NECK:  Free range of motion without thyromegaly.,CHEST:  Clear to auscultation without wheeze or rhonchi.,HEART:  Regular rate and rhythm without murmur, gallop, or rub.,ABDOMEN:  Soft, nontender.,MUSCULOSKELETAL:  There is musculoskeletal soreness and tenderness found at the ankles, feet, as well as the low back, particularly above the SI joints bilaterally.  Passive hip motion also elicits bilateral hip pain referred to the ipsilateral side.  Toe-heel walking is performed without difficulty.  Straight leg raises are negative.  Romberg's are negative.,NEUROLOGIC:  Grossly intact.  Intact reflexes in all extremities tested.  Romberg is negative and downgoing.,

llm_plan: ASSESSMENT: Multilevel cervical spinal stenosis with progressive cervical myelopathy and bilateral cervical radiculopathy, right greater than left. The patient presents with clinical and radiographic findings consistent with moderate to severe degenerative cervical myelopathy. MRI demonstrates moderate stenosis at C4-5 and C5-6 with bilateral neural foraminal stenosis and significant disk herniation at C6-7, with effacement of ventral and dorsal CSF spaces at C4-5 and C5-6. Physical examination reveals bilateral upper extremity weakness (4/5 grip strength, 4/5 hand intrinsics, 4+/5 proximal muscle groups), sensory deficits in C6 distribution bilaterally (right greater than left), and hyperreflexia (3+ biceps and brachioradialis reflexes). The patient has progressive functional decline with difficulty performing activities of daily living. Lower extremity examination is reassuring with normal strength, normal gait, and absence of clonus or pathologic Hoffmann sign, though hyperreflexia (3+ patellar reflexes) is present. The absence of bowel/bladder dysfunction is favorable, but the progressive motor weakness, bilateral radiculopathy, and multilevel cord compression indicate advancing disease requiring surgical evaluation. PLAN: Neurosurgery referral: Urgent referral to spine surgery for evaluation of surgical decompression and stabilization. Given the progressive motor weakness, bilateral radiculopathy with functional impairment, and multilevel cord compression with CSF effacement on MRI, the patient meets criteria for surgical intervention. Activity modification: Counsel patient to avoid high-risk activities that could result in cervical spine trauma or hyperextension/hyperflexion injuries. Avoid contact sports, heavy lifting, and activities requiring overhead work. Pain management: Continue current physical therapy for neck pain. Consider addition of: NSAIDs (if not contraindicated) for anti-inflammatory effect and pain control Gabapentin 300 mg PO TID, titrate as needed for neuropathic radicular pain Short course of oral corticosteroids may be considered if radicular symptoms are severe Monitoring: Instruct patient to return immediately or go to emergency department if develops: Worsening weakness, particularly in lower extremities New onset bowel or bladder dysfunction Gait instability or falls Rapid progression of upper extremity weakness Follow-up: Schedule follow-up appointment in 2-4 weeks or sooner if symptoms worsen, to review neurosurgery recommendations and coordinate care.

presentation: SUBJECTIVE:  ,The patient seeks evaluation for a second opinion concerning cataract extraction.  She tells me cataract extraction has been recommended in each eye; however, she is nervous to have surgery.  Past ocular surgery history is significant for neurovascular age-related macular degeneration. llm_plan: ASSESSMENT: Bilateral cataracts (early nuclear sclerosis OU with 1-2+ posterior subcapsular cataract OS) in the setting of active neovascular age-related macular degeneration OU The patient presents with severely reduced vision (20/400 OU) that does not improve with refraction. While cataracts are present bilaterally, the primary driver of her poor visual acuity is likely the active neovascular AMD with choroidal neovascularization, subretinal hemorrhage, and blood in both eyes. The cataracts described are relatively mild and would not typically account for vision this poor. The presence of active CNV with hemorrhage indicates inadequately controlled wet AMD that requires optimization before considering cataract surgery. PLAN: Optimize neovascular AMD treatment first: Coordinate with Dr. X (retina specialist) to ensure patient is receiving appropriate anti-VEGF therapy Goal is to achieve disease stability with resolution of subretinal hemorrhage and control of CNV activity Evidence suggests at least 6 months of anti-VEGF therapy before cataract surgery is associated with optimal visual outcomes Defer cataract surgery at this time: Cataract surgery should be postponed until wet AMD is adequately controlled Reassure patient that cataract surgery does not worsen AMD progression and can provide meaningful visual improvement even in patients with wet AMD Set realistic expectations that final visual outcome will depend on macular status Patient counseling: Discussed that her poor vision is primarily due to active wet AMD rather than cataracts alone Explained importance of controlling AMD first to maximize potential benefit from future cataract surgery Addressed her surgical anxiety and reassured her that when the time is appropriate, cataract surgery can be performed safely Follow-up: Continue regular follow-up with retina specialist for anti-VEGF injections Reassess candidacy for cataract surgery once AMD activity is controlled for at least 6 months Patient may return for cataract surgery evaluation once retina specialist confirms disease stability

Bilateral cataracts (early nuclear sclerosis OU with 1-2+ posterior subcapsular cataract OS)

Aripiprazole can be titrated up to 15 mg/day if needed. Coordinate care with school, ABCD providers, and psychologists to ensure consistent behavioral strategies across settings. Follow-up in 4-6 weeks to reassess behavioral symptoms, medication tolerability, review functional behavioral analysis results when available, and adjust treatment plan accordingly.

llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: 1. The patient has clinical findings suggestive of cervical myelopathy including bilateral upper extremity weakness (4+/5 strength), tremor, slow gait with short steps, and pain. Significant unintentional weight loss (35 pounds over one year, 24% body weight loss) This degree of weight loss is highly concerning and requires comprehensive evaluation. Malignancy, nonmalignant gastrointestinal disease, and psychosocial disorders are common etiologies. Her difficulty swallowing raises concern for esophageal pathology. Depression is a known contributor. 3. Possible cervical myelopathy Clinical findings concerning for myelopathy include bilateral upper extremity weakness, tremor, slow gait with short steps, and difficulty swallowing. However, Hoffmann's sign is negative and reflexes are normal. 4. Uncontrolled hypertension (BP 138/78) Despite history of hypertension, patient reports no current medications. 5. presentation: SUBJECTIVE:,  This is a 62-year-old female who comes for dietary consultation for carbohydrate counting for type I diabetes.  The patient reports that she was hospitalized over the weekend for DKA.  She indicates that her blood sugar on Friday night was 187 at bedtime and that when she woke up in the morning her blood sugar was 477.  She gave herself, in smaller increments, a total of 70 extra units of her Humalog.  Ten of those units were injectable; the others were in the forms of pump.  Her blood sugar was over 600 when she went to the hospital later that day.  She is here at this consultation complaining of not feeling well still because she has a cold.  She realizes that this is likely because her immune system was so minimized in the hospital.,OBJECTIVE:,  Current insulin doses on her insulin pump are boluses set at 5 units at breakfast, 6 units at lunch and 11 units at supper.  Her basal rates have not been changed since her last visit with Charla Yassine and totaled 30.5 units per 24 hours.  A diet history was obtained.  I instructed the patient on carbohydrate counting at 1 unit of insulin for every 10 g carbohydrate ratio was recommended.  A correction dose of approximately 1 unit of insulin to bring the blood sugars down 30 mg/dl was also recommended.  The Lilly guide for meal planning was provided and reviewed.  Additional carbohydrate counting book was provided.,
human_ap: ASSESSMENT:,  The patient was taught an insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio of 1 unit to 10 g of carbohydrates as recommended at the previous visit two years ago, which she does not recall.  It is based on the 500 rule which suggests this ratio.  We did identify carbohydrate sources in the food supply, recognizing 15-g equivalents.  We also identified the need to dose her insulin at the time that she is eating her carbohydrate sources.  She does seem to have a pattern of fixing blood sugars later in the day after they are elevated.  We discussed the other option of trying to eat a consistent amount of carbohydrates at meals from day to day and taking a consistent amount of insulin at those meals.  With this in mind, she was recommended to follow with three servings or 45 g of carbohydrate at breakfast, three servings or 45 g of carbohydrate at lunch and four servings or 60 g of carbohydrate at dinner.  Joanne Araiza joined our consultation briefly to discuss whether her pump was working appropriately.  The patient was given an 800 number for the pump to contact should there be any question about its failure to deliver insulin appropriately.,PLAN:,  Recommend the patient use 1 unit of insulin for every 10-g carbohydrate load consumed.  Recommend the patient either use this as a carbohydrate counting tool or work harder at keeping carbohydrate content consistent at meals from day to day.  This was a one-hour consultation.  Provided my name and number should additional needs arise.
human_dx_summary: The patient is being managed with an insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio of 1 unit per 10 grams of carbohydrates to optimize blood sugar control and improve insulin dosing timing.
llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with recent diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), now resolved. This 62-year-old female with type 1 diabetes on insulin pump therapy presented for dietary consultation following hospitalization for DKA over the weekend. The precipitating event appears to be pump malfunction or infusion set failure, given the rapid rise in blood glucose from 187 mg/dL at bedtime to 477 mg/dL in the morning despite administration of 70 units of Humalog. The lack of response to pump-delivered insulin strongly suggests interruption of insulin delivery. The patient's current upper respiratory infection likely contributed to increased insulin requirements and metabolic stress. Current insulin regimen includes basal rate of 30.5 units per 24 hours and fixed boluses (5 units breakfast, 6 units lunch, 11 units dinner) totaling approximately 52.5 units daily. PLAN: Diabetes Management: Insulin pump settings: Continue current basal rate of 30.5 units/24 hours. Verify pump function and infusion set integrity. Educate patient on recognition of pump malfunction. Insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio: Implement 1:10 ratio (1 unit per 10 grams carbohydrate) as recommended. Correction factor: Implement 1 unit to lower blood glucose by 30 mg/dL as recommended. Sick day management: Provide written sick day protocol including: more frequent blood glucose monitoring (every 2-4 hours), ketone monitoring when blood glucose >250 mg/dL, increased fluid intake, continuation of basal insulin even if not eating, and criteria for seeking urgent care. Monitoring: Blood glucose monitoring: Continue frequent monitoring, especially during current illness Ketone monitoring: Check blood or urine ketones if blood glucose >250 mg/dL or with illness symptoms Pump site inspection: Change infusion set every 2-3 days and rotate sites Education: Carbohydrate counting education provided today with Lilly guide and additional resources Reinforce importance of never stopping basal insulin Review pump troubleshooting: if blood glucose remains elevated after 2 correction boluses, change infusion set and consider backup injection Provide backup insulin pen (long-acting and rapid-acting) for pump failures Follow-up: Follow up in 1-2 weeks to review blood glucose logs and assess response to new insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio and correction factor Consider continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) if not already using Schedule endocrinology follow-up within 3 months Current Illness: Supportive care for upper respiratory infection: rest, hydration, over-the-counter symptom management as needed

llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: This is a 75-year-old female presenting with acute onset left-sided facial weakness, facial numbness, and hand numbness concerning for either peripheral facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy) versus central nervous system pathology (stroke/TIA). Findings favoring peripheral facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy): Acute onset over hours, recent earache (common prodrome), history of recent dizziness/vertigo, no uvula or tongue deviation, symmetric muscle strength and reflexes bilaterally, no other focal neurologic deficits. Risk factors requiring consideration of central pathology: Age 75, left hand numbness, elevated blood pressure 175/86, low oxygen saturation 93%, history of recent fall with dizziness, nausea. Most likely diagnosis: Peripheral facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy), but stroke/TIA must be excluded given age, vascular risk factors, and atypical features. PLAN: Immediate Actions: STAT non-contrast head CT to exclude intracranial hemorrhage, acute stroke, or mass lesion If CT negative, obtain brain MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging within 24 hours Point-of-care glucose to exclude hypoglycemia ECG and continuous telemetry monitoring to screen for atrial fibrillation Supplemental oxygen to maintain saturation >94% Laboratory Studies: Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel Hemoglobin A1c and lipid panel Troponin Consider Lyme serology if in endemic area Additional Workup: Carotid duplex ultrasound or CT angiography of head and neck Echocardiogram Treatment: If imaging excludes stroke and confirms peripheral facial nerve palsy: Prednisone 60 mg PO daily for 5 days, then taper over 5 days Consider adding valacyclovir 1 g PO three times daily for 7 days Eye protection: artificial tears during day, ophthalmic lubricating ointment at night Ophthalmology referral if unable to close eye completely If imaging demonstrates acute stroke/TIA: Neurology consultation (emergent) Antiplatelet therapy per neurology recommendations Admit for stroke workup and secondary prevention Disposition: Admit for urgent stroke workup versus observation unit with expedited imaging Neurology consultation Follow-up: If Bell's palsy confirmed: follow up in 1 week to assess response Physical therapy referral if severe paralysis persists

llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: 71-year-old male with perioperative hypertension following laser prostate surgery. The patient has a history of chronic hypertension previously controlled on atenolol and lisinopril, which were discontinued by his cardiologist several months ago. Preoperative blood pressure was severely elevated at 181/107 mmHg, requiring IV labetalol. Postoperative blood pressure remains elevated at 158/100 mmHg. The patient is currently asymptomatic without chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, or neurologic symptoms, suggesting this represents perioperative hypertension without acute target organ damage rather than a hypertensive emergency. Contributing factors include postoperative pain, anxiety, bladder distention, withdrawal from chronic antihypertensive medications, and possible inadequate thyroid replacement. PLAN: Blood Pressure Management: Assess and address reversible causes: Ensure adequate pain control, evaluate for urinary retention/bladder distention, assess volume status Continue monitoring blood pressure closely Restart oral antihypertensive therapy as soon as patient is tolerating oral intake. Consider restarting atenolol 25-50 mg daily and lisinopril 10-20 mg daily (pending discussion with cardiology regarding reason for discontinuation) Target blood pressure <130/80 mmHg If blood pressure remains >=160/90 mmHg, consider short-acting IV antihypertensive while transitioning to oral therapy Thyroid Function: Check TSH and free T4 to ensure adequate thyroid replacement on current levothyroxine dose Cardiovascular Risk Assessment: Obtain baseline ECG to assess for atrial fibrillation recurrence and any ischemic changes Basic metabolic panel to assess renal function and electrolytes prior to restarting ACE inhibitor Postoperative Care: Continue routine post-TURP care including monitoring for hematuria and ensuring adequate urine output Ensure adequate pain control to minimize sympathetic stimulation Follow-up: Cardiology consultation to discuss rationale for prior discontinuation of antihypertensives and optimal long-term blood pressure management Primary care follow-up within 1-2 weeks of discharge for blood pressure monitoring and medication titration
llm_diagnoses: Perioperative hypertension following laser prostate surgery
llm_dx_summary: A 71-year-old male with perioperative hypertension after laser prostate surgery, likely due to withdrawal of chronic antihypertensive medications and other reversible factors, currently asymptomatic without evidence of acute target organ damage.

llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: 1. Multiple lacerations to right hand, third, fourth, and fifth metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints - concerning for "fight bite" (clenched-fist injury) with high risk of joint capsule penetration This 19-year-old male sustained lacerations over the MCP joints after punching someone in the mouth/face, which is the classic mechanism for a clenched-fist injury. These injuries carry significant risk because the tooth may have penetrated the extensor tendon and joint capsule. The patient has full range of motion and no gross deformities, and x-rays show no fracture. However, the joint capsule is penetrated in approximately 96% of fight bite injuries involving the MCP joint, even when not initially apparent. These wounds are at extremely high risk for polymicrobial infection. 2. Elevated blood pressure (161/98 mmHg) Likely secondary to pain, stress, and alcohol intoxication. PLAN: 1. Fight bite injuries: Hand surgery consultation: Immediate consultation with hand surgery or orthopedics is indicated for surgical exploration to assess for joint capsule penetration, extensor tendon injury, and thorough debridement. Antibiotics: Continue amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg PO twice daily for 5-7 days. Appropriate coverage for Eikenella corrodens and polymicrobial flora. Wound care: Keep wounds clean and dry. Elevate hand above heart level. Monitor closely for signs of infection. Immobilization: Splint hand in position of function pending hand surgery evaluation. Pain management: Ibuprofen 600 mg PO every 6 hours as needed. Tetanus: Confirmed up-to-date. 2. Follow-up: Urgent hand surgery evaluation within 24 hours, ideally today. If managed non-operatively, close follow-up within 24-48 hours to reassess for infection. Return precautions: fever, increasing pain, redness spreading, purulent drainage, inability to move fingers, or numbness/tingling. Suture removal in 10-14 days. 3. Blood pressure: Recheck when patient is sober and pain-free. If persistently elevated, outpatient follow-up for evaluation. 4. Alcohol use: Brief counseling provided regarding risks. DISPOSITION: Patient requires urgent hand surgery consultation today. Low threshold for surgical exploration given high risk of serious complications.

llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN Assessment: 45-year-old woman with history of papillary thyroid carcinoma status post total thyroidectomy (1992), acquired hypothyroidism on levothyroxine replacement, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and obstructive sleep apnea on CPAP, presenting for routine endocrine follow-up with chief complaint of daytime fatigue. Papillary thyroid carcinoma, status post total thyroidectomy (1992) - stable, no evidence of recurrence. Thyroglobulin is undetectable (<0.5) with negative thyroglobulin antibodies (<20). TSH is appropriately suppressed at 0.121. No palpable thyroid tissue or cervical lymphadenopathy. Recurrence risk is very low given >30 years from initial surgery with consistently undetectable thyroglobulin. Acquired hypothyroidism on levothyroxine - adequately replaced. Free T4 is 1.35 (within normal range). No clinical signs of hypothyroidism or thyrotoxicosis. Note: medication list appears to list both levothyroxine 125 mcg and Synthroid - likely documentation duplication, needs clarification. Daytime fatigue. Patient reports feeling refreshed upon waking with CPAP but fatiguing later in the day. Thyroid labs are at goal and do not explain this symptom. Differential includes suboptimal CPAP compliance/efficacy, diabetes-related fatigue, medication side effects, deconditioning, iron deficiency, vitamin D deficiency, or depression. Type 2 diabetes mellitus. Currently on triple therapy with glipizide, Avandamet, and Byetta. No recent HbA1c available. Plan: Thyroid cancer surveillance: Continue levothyroxine 125 mcg daily Clarify medication duplication Continue TSH suppression to goal <0.5; current level 0.121 is appropriate Repeat thyroglobulin, thyroglobulin antibody, and TSH in 12 months Consider discussion regarding whether degree of TSH suppression can be relaxed Neck ultrasound if not performed recently Fatigue workup: Obtain CBC, ferritin, iron studies, vitamin B12, vitamin D level, comprehensive metabolic panel, and HbA1c Screen for depression (PHQ-9) Review CPAP compliance data; consider referral back to sleep medicine if suboptimal Diabetes management: Obtain HbA1c and fasting lipid panel Note that rosiglitazone (component of Avandamet) carries cardiovascular and fracture risk concerns; consider transitioning to regimen without rosiglitazone Review home glucose logs Blood pressure: Systolic 135 mmHg today - borderline elevated Recheck at next visit; if persistently elevated, consider ACE inhibitor or ARB given diabetes Follow-up: Return to endocrine clinic in 6 months with labs drawn prior to visit
llm_diagnoses: Papillary thyroid carcinoma, status post total thyroidectomy (stable, no evidence of recurrence)
llm_dx_summary: A 45-year-old woman with stable papillary thyroid carcinoma post-thyroidectomy, adequately treated hypothyroidism, type 2 diabetes, and obstructive sleep apnea presents with daytime fatigue likely multifactorial and unrelated to thyroid status.

llm_plan: ASSESSMENT: Persistent allergic rhinitis, inadequately controlled on oral antihistamine monotherapy This 23-year-old female presents with persistent allergic rhinitis symptoms that have failed to respond adequately to multiple oral second-generation antihistamines (loratadine, cetirizine, and fexofenadine). Physical examination findings of erythematous and swollen nasal mucosa with clear drainage are consistent with allergic rhinitis. Her asthma is well-controlled and not currently contributing to her symptoms. PLAN: Medications: Discontinue Allegra (fexofenadine) Start fluticasone propionate nasal spray 2 sprays each nostril once daily. Counsel on proper technique: direct spray away from nasal septum. Advise that full therapeutic effect may take several days to weeks. Consider adding intranasal azelastine if symptoms do not improve adequately after 2-3 weeks, or may consider combination azelastine-fluticasone (Dymista) as alternative Continue Ortho Tri-Cyclen Non-pharmacologic measures: Recommend saline nasal irrigation Discuss environmental allergen avoidance strategies Follow-up: Return to clinic in 4-6 weeks to assess response If symptoms remain inadequately controlled despite optimal intranasal therapy, consider referral to Allergy/Immunology for skin testing and potential allergen immunotherapy Patient education: Discussed that intranasal corticosteroids are more effective than oral antihistamines for persistent allergic rhinitis Counseled on proper nasal spray technique Advised to watch for epistaxis Instructed to use medication daily for best results rather than as needed

presentation: CHIEF COMPLAINT: , Motor vehicle accident.,HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: , This is a 32-year-old Hispanic female who presents to the emergency department today via ambulance.  The patient was brought by ambulance following a motor vehicle collision approximately 45 minutes ago.  The patient states that she was driving her vehicle at approximately 40 miles per hour.  The patient was driving a minivan.  The patient states that the car in front of her stopped too quickly and she rear-ended the vehicle ahead of her.  The patient states that she was wearing her seatbelt.  She was driving.  There were no other passengers in the van.  The patient states that she was restrained by the seatbelt and that her airbag deployed.  The patient denies hitting her head.  She states that she does have some mild pain on the left aspect of her neck.  The patient states that she believes she may have passed out shortly after the accident.  The patient states that she also has some pain low in her abdomen that she believes is likely due to the steering wheel or deployment on the airbag.  The patient denies any pain in her knees, ankles, or feet.  She denies any pain in her shoulders, elbows, and wrists.  The patient does state that she is somewhat painful throughout the bones of her pelvis as well.  The patient did not walk after this accident.  She was removed from her car and placed on a backboard and immobilized.  The patient denies any chest pain or difficulty breathing.  She denies any open lacerations or abrasions.  The patient has not had any headache, nausea or vomiting.  She has not felt feverish or chilled.  The patient does states that there is significant deformity to the front of the vehicle that she was driving, which again was a minivan.  There were no oblique vectors or force placed on this accident.  The patient had straight rear-ending of the vehicle in front of her. llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: Large local reaction to hymenoptera (bee) stings. The patient presents with localized edema and erythema to the left hand following multiple bee stings approximately 6 hours ago. The reaction is confined to the sting site without any systemic manifestations such as urticaria, angioedema, respiratory symptoms, or cardiovascular compromise. This represents a large local reaction rather than anaphylaxis. The absence of immediate reaction and development of progressive swelling over several hours is consistent with an IgE-mediated late-phase inflammatory response. Vital signs are stable, airway is patent, and there are no signs of systemic involvement. PLAN: Medications: Continue loratadine 10 mg orally once daily for 3-5 days for symptomatic relief Prednisone 40 mg orally once daily for 3-5 days to reduce inflammation and swelling Ibuprofen 400-600 mg orally every 6-8 hours as needed for pain Apply cold compresses to affected area for comfort Patient Education: Reassure patient that large local reactions are self-limited and typically resolve within 3-10 days Advise that swelling is due to inflammatory mediator release, not infection; antibiotics are not indicated unless signs of secondary infection develop Discuss insect avoidance strategies Epinephrine Auto-Injector: Prescription for epinephrine auto-injector 0.3 mg is optional for large local reactions but may be considered given the patient's age and cardiac history If prescribed, provide education on recognition of systemic symptoms and proper administration technique Follow-up: Return to ED or call 911 immediately if develops any signs of systemic reaction Follow up with primary care physician in 3-5 days if swelling is not improving or if signs of infection develop Consider referral to allergist if patient experiences recurrent large local reactions Monitoring: Patient may be discharged home with close observation by family No indication for venom-specific IgE testing or venom immunotherapy at this time

llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: Acute urticaria, likely idiopathic versus possible delayed irritant contact dermatitis from fiberglass insulation exposure. This 34-year-old male presents with acute onset generalized pruritic urticarial rash involving torso, arms, and buttocks with no angioedema or respiratory compromise. The patient responded well to epinephrine and diphenhydramine in the ED. While no clear trigger is identified, the recent exposure to insulation material 2 days prior raises the possibility of delayed irritant contact dermatitis from fiberglass. The absence of facial/oropharyngeal swelling, respiratory symptoms, and hemodynamic instability argues against anaphylaxis. Given the acute presentation, extensive laboratory workup is not indicated at this time. PLAN: Medications: Prescribe cetirizine 10 mg PO daily for 7-10 days (second-generation H1-antihistamine preferred for fewer sedating effects) Prescribe prednisone 40 mg PO daily for 3-5 days (short course given severity of presentation) Provide EpiPen prescription with instructions for use if symptoms recur with facial swelling, throat tightness, or difficulty breathing Trigger Avoidance: Avoid further exposure to insulation materials until symptoms completely resolve Review potential triggers including new foods, medications, supplements, or environmental exposures Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin given multiple drug allergies and potential to exacerbate urticaria Patient Education: Discussed that acute urticaria is typically self-limited and resolves within 6 weeks Instructed to seek immediate emergency care for any signs of angioedema or respiratory symptoms Advised on proper clothing and protective equipment if future insulation work is necessary Follow-up: Return to clinic or ED immediately if symptoms worsen, develop angioedema, or respiratory symptoms Routine follow-up in 1-2 weeks if symptoms persist or recur If urticaria persists beyond 6 weeks, will consider limited laboratory evaluation (CBC with differential, ESR/CRP) and possible allergy referral Diagnostic Testing: No laboratory testing indicated at this time given typical presentation and good response to treatment

llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: Acute gastroenteritis with dehydration and prerenal acute kidney injury, complicated by hyperkalemia This 85-year-old female presents with acute diarrhea and vomiting consistent with acute gastroenteritis. Prerenal acute kidney injury is present with BUN 54 mg/dL, creatinine 2.2 mg/dL (BUN:Cr ratio ~25:1), consistent with volume depletion from gastrointestinal losses. Hyperkalemia (K+ 6.1 mEq/L) is concerning and likely multifactorial: prerenal AKI with reduced renal potassium excretion, possible medication effects, and metabolic acidosis (bicarb 20). The prolonged QT interval on EKG is particularly worrisome in the setting of hyperkalemia and warrants urgent treatment. Mild leukocytosis (WBC 11.2) may reflect dehydration, stress response, or infectious process. PLAN: 1. Hyperkalemia Management (URGENT): Calcium gluconate 1-2 grams IV over 2-5 minutes for cardiac membrane stabilization Regular insulin 10 units IV with dextrose 50% (25g) IV Albuterol 10-20 mg via nebulizer Continuous cardiac monitoring Repeat potassium level in 1-2 hours Serial glucose monitoring 2. Acute Kidney Injury and Dehydration: IV fluid resuscitation: Lactated Ringer's or normal saline, initial bolus 500-1000 mL Monitor urine output (consider Foley catheter) Repeat BMP in 4-6 hours Avoid nephrotoxic agents Review and hold home medications - particularly RAAS inhibitors, diuretics, NSAIDs 3. Gastroenteritis: Stool studies: C. difficile PCR, stool culture, consider multiplex GI PCR panel Supportive care: ondansetron 4 mg IV PRN for nausea NPO initially, advance to clear liquids as tolerated Contact precautions pending stool studies No antibiotics at this time unless specific pathogen identified 4. Diabetes Management: Hold oral hypoglycemics until taking PO and renal function clarified Insulin sliding scale for glucose management 5. Medication Reconciliation: Obtain accurate medication list from pharmacy/family 6. Monitoring and Disposition: Telemetry monitoring given hyperkalemia and prolonged QT Admission to monitored bed Serial labs: BMP in 4-6 hours, then daily 7. Follow-up: Nephrology consultation if AKI does not improve with hydration Cardiology consultation if QT prolongation persists Outpatient follow-up with PCP within 1 week of discharge

presentation: CHIEF COMPLAINT: , Newly diagnosed high-risk acute lymphoblastic leukemia; extensive deep vein thrombosis, right iliac vein and inferior vena cava (IVC), status post balloon angioplasty, and mechanical and pharmacologic thrombolysis following placement of a vena caval filter.,HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: , The patient was transferred here the evening of 02/23/2007 from Hospital with a new diagnosis of high-risk acute lymphoblastic leukemia based on confirmation by flow cytometry of peripheral blood lymphoblasts that afternoon.  History related to this illness probably dates back to October of 2006 when he had onset of swelling and discomfort in the left testicle with what he described as a residual "lump" posteriorly.  The left testicle has continued to be painful off and on since.  In early November, he developed pain in the posterior part of his upper right leg, which he initially thought was related to skateboarding and muscle strain.  Physical therapy was prescribed and the discomfort temporarily improved.  In December, he noted onset of increasing fatigue.  He used to work out regularly, lifting lifts, doing abdominal exercises, and playing basketball and found he did not have energy to pursue these activities.  He has lost 10 pounds since December and feels his appetite has decreased.  Night sweats and cough began in December, for which he was treated with a course of Augmentin.  However, both of these problems have continued.  He also began taking Accutane for persistent acne in December (this agent was stopped on 02/19/2007).  Despite increasing fatigue and lethargy, he continues his studies at University of Denver, has a biology major (he aspires to be an ophthalmologist).,The morning of 02/19/2007, he awakened with severe right inguinal and right lower quadrant pain.  He was seen in Emergency Room where it was noted that he had an elevated WBC of 18,000.  CT scan of the abdomen was obtained to rule out possible appendicitis and on that CT, a large clot in the inferior vena cava extending to the right iliac and femoral veins was found.  He promptly underwent appropriate treatment in interventional radiology with the above-noted angioplasty and placement of a vena caval filter followed by mechanical and pharmacologic thrombolysis.  Repeat ultrasound there on 02/20/2007 showed no evidence of deep venous thrombosis (DVT).  Continuous intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion was continued.  Because there was no obvious cause of this extensive thrombosis, occult malignancy was suspected.  Appropriate blood studies were obtained and he underwent a PET/CT scan as part of his diagnostic evaluation.  This study showed moderately increased diffuse bone marrow metabolic activity.  Because the WBC continued to rise and showed a preponderance of lymphocytes, the smear was reviewed by pathologist, Sheryl Asplund, M.D., and flow cytometry was performed on the peripheral blood.  These studies became available the afternoon of 02/23/2007, and confirmed the diagnosis of precursor-B acute lymphoblastic leukemia.  The patient was transferred here after stopping of the continuous infusion heparin and receiving a dose of Lovenox 60 mg subcutaneously for further diagnostic evaluation and management of the acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).,ALLERGIES: , NO KNOWN DRUG ALLERGIES.  HE DOES SEEM TO REACT TO CERTAIN ADHESIVES.,CURRENT MEDICATIONS:  ,1.  Lovenox 60 mg subcutaneously q.12h. initiated.,2.  Coumadin 5 mg p.o., was administered on 02/19/2007 and 02/22/2007.,3.  Protonix 40 mg intravenous (IV) daily.,4.  Vicodin p.r.n.,5.  Levaquin 750 mg IV on 02/23/2007.,IMMUNIZATIONS: , Up-to-date.,PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:  ,The treatment of the thrombosis as noted above on 02/19/2007 and 02/20/2007.,FAMILY HISTORY:  ,Two half-brothers, ages 26 and 28, both in good health.  Parents are in good health.  A maternal great-grandmother had a deep venous thrombosis (DVT) of leg in her 40s.  A maternal great-uncle developed leukemia around age 50.  A maternal great-grandfather had bone cancer around age 80.  His paternal grandfather died of colon cancer at age 73, which he had had since age 68.  Adult-onset diabetes is present in distant relatives on both sides.,SOCIAL HISTORY:  ,The patient is a student at the University majoring in biology.  He lives in a dorm there.  His parents live in Breckenridge.  He admits to having smoked marijuana off and on with friends and drinking beer off and on as well.,REVIEW OF SYSTEMS: , He has had emesis off and on related to Vicodin and constipation since 02/19/2007, also related to pain medication.  He has had acne for about two years, which he describes as mild to moderate.  He denied shortness of breath, chest pain, hemoptysis, dyspnea, headaches, joint pains, rashes, except where he has had dressings applied, and extremity pain except for the right leg pain noted above.,PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:  ,GENERAL:  Alert, cooperative, moderately ill-appearing young man.,VITAL SIGNS:  At the time of admission, pulse was 94, respirations 20, blood pressure 120/62, temperature 98.7, height 171.5 cm, weight 63.04 kg, and pulse oximetry on room air 95%.,HAIR AND SKIN:  Mild facial acne.,HEENT:  Extraocular muscles (EOMs) intact.  Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light and accommodation (PERRLA), fundi normal.,CARDIOVASCULAR:  A 2/6 systolic ejection murmur (SEM), regular sinus rhythm (RSR).,LUNGS:  Clear to auscultation with an occasional productive cough.,ABDOMEN:  Soft with mild lower quadrant tenderness, right more so than left; liver and spleen each decreased 4 cm below their respective costal margins.,MUSCULOSKELETAL:  Mild swelling of the dorsal aspect of the right foot and distal right leg.  Mild tenderness over the prior catheter entrance site in the right popliteal fossa and mild tenderness over the right medial upper thigh.,GENITOURINARY:  Testicle exam disclosed no firm swelling with mild nondiscrete fullness in the posterior left testicle.,NEUROLOGIC:  Exam showed him to be oriented x4.  Normal fundi, intact cranial nerves II through XII with downgoing toes, symmetric muscle strength, and decreased patellar deep tendon reflexes (DTRs).,LABORATORY DATA:  ,White count 25,500 (26 neutrophils, 1 band, 7 lymphocytes, 1 monocyte, 1 myelocyte, 64 blasts), hemoglobin 13.3, hematocrit 38.8, and 312,000 platelets. llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: Newly diagnosed high-risk precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) A 20-year-old male presenting with constitutional symptoms (fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, cough), hepatosplenomegaly, peripheral blasts (64% on differential), and markedly elevated LDH (1925) with flow cytometry confirming precursor-B ALL. He is classified as an adolescent/young adult (AYA) patient. Risk stratification is pending cytogenetic and molecular characterization. Extensive deep vein thrombosis, right iliac vein and IVC, status post balloon angioplasty, mechanical and pharmacologic thrombolysis, and IVC filter placement Likely multifactorial etiology: hypercoagulable state associated with underlying malignancy, possible contribution from prior isotretinoin use, and family history of DVT. Currently on enoxaparin 60 mg subQ q12h and warfarin 5 mg with subtherapeutic INR (1.2). Possible left testicular involvement History of left testicular swelling dating back to October 2006 with current exam showing mild nondiscrete fullness. PLAN: Problem 1: Precursor B-cell ALL Complete diagnostic workup: Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with morphology, flow cytometry, and MRD characterization Karyotype with G-banded metaphase chromosomes FISH panel including BCR::ABL1, KMT2A rearrangements RT-PCR for BCR::ABL1 Next-generation sequencing Additional workup: Hepatitis B/C and HIV testing, echocardiogram prior to anthracycline therapy, scrotal ultrasound, lumbar puncture with intrathecal chemotherapy Fertility counseling and sperm banking prior to chemotherapy Central venous access device placement Initiate early transplant evaluation and donor search Tumor lysis syndrome prophylaxis: aggressive IV hydration, allopurinol or rasburicase; monitor every 6-8 hours Induction chemotherapy: pending cytogenetic results. presentation: CHIEF COMPLAINT:, Blood-borne pathogen exposure., ,HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: ,The patient is a 54-year-old right-handed male who works as a phlebotomist and respiratory therapist at Hospital. The patient states that he was attempting to do a blood gas. He had his finger of the left hand over the pulse and was inserting a needle using the right hand. He did have a protective clothing including use of gloves at the time of the incident. As he advanced the needle, the patient jerked away, this caused him to pull out of the arm and inadvertently pricked the tip of his index finger. The patient was seen and evaluated at the emergency department at the time of incident and had baseline studies drawn, and has been followed by employee health for his injury. The source patient was tested for signs of disease and was found to be negative for HIV, but was found to be a carrier for hepatitis C. The patient has had periodic screening including a blood tests and returns now for his final exam., ,REVIEW OF SYSTEMS: ,The patient prior to today has been very well without any signs or symptoms of viral illness, but yesterday he began to experience symptoms of nausea, had an episode of vomiting last night. Has low appetite. There were no fevers, chills, or malaise. No headache. No congestion or cold. No coughing. He had no sore throat. There was no chest pain or troubled breathing. He did have abdominal symptoms as described above but no abdominal pain. There were no urinary symptoms. No darkening of the skin or eyes. He had no yellowing or darkening of the urine. He had no rash to the skin. There was no local infection at the side of the fingerstick. All other systems were negative., ,PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: ,Significant for degenerative disc disease in the back., ,MEDICATIONS: ,Nexium., ,ALLERGIES:, IV contrast., ,CURRENT WORK STATUS:, He continues on full duty work., ,PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:, The patient was awake and alert. He was seated upright. He did not appear ill or toxic, and was well hydrated. His temperature was 97.2 degrees, pulse was 84, respirations 14 and unlabored, and blood pressure 102/70. HEENT exam, the sclerae were clear. Ocular movements were full and intact. His oropharynx was clear. There was no pharyngeal erythema. No tonsillar enlargement. His neck was supple and nontender. He had no masses. There was no adenopathy in his cervical or axillary chain. Breath sounds were clear and equal without wheeze or rales. Heart tones were regular without murmur or gallop. His abdomen was soft, flat, and nontender. There was no enlargement of the liver or spleen. His extremities were without rash or edema. He had normal gait and balance without ataxia., ,
human_ap: ASSESSMENT: ,The patient presents for evaluation after a contaminated needlestick to the index finger. The source patient was tested and found to be negative for HIV. However, he did test positive for hepatitis C. He was described as a carrier without active disease. The patient has been followed with periodic evaluation including blood testing. He has completed a 3 shot series for hepatitis B and had titers drawn that showed protected antibodies. He also was up-to-date on his immunization including tetanus. The patient has been well during this time except for the onset of a intestinal illness being investigated with some squeakiness and vomiting. He had no other symptoms that were suggestive of acute hepatitis. His abdominal exam was normal. He had no generalized lymphadenopathy and no fever. Blood tests were drawn on 02/07/2005. The results of which were reviewed with the patient. His liver function test was normal at 18. His hepatitis C and HIV, both of which were negative. He had no local signs of infection, and otherwise has been doing well except for his acute intestinal illness as described above., ,IMPRESSION:, Blood-borne pathogen exposure secondary to contaminated needlestick., ,PLAN: ,The patient is now six months out from his injury. He had negative lab studies. There were no physical findings that were suggestive of disease transmission. He was counseled on ways to prevent exposure in the future including use of protective gear including gloves, which he states that he always does. He was counseled that ways to prevent transmission or exposure to intimate contacts., ,WORK STATUS:, He was released to regular work., ,CONDITION: ,He was reassured that no signs of disease transmission had occurred as result of his injury. He therefore was found to be medically stationary without signs of impairment of today's date.

llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: Occupational needlestick exposure to hepatitis C virus (HCV)-positive source patient, now at final follow-up visit (approximately 4-6 months post-exposure). The patient has completed appropriate serial testing per CDC guidelines. The recent episode of nausea and vomiting is most likely unrelated to HCV infection given the timing and lack of other symptoms consistent with acute hepatitis C. PLAN: Laboratory Testing: Anti-HCV antibody testing today (final test at 4-6 months post-exposure per CDC guidelines) Hepatic function panel (ALT, AST, bilirubin) to assess for any subclinical hepatitis Results Interpretation and Follow-up: If anti-HCV antibody is negative and liver enzymes are normal, the patient can be reassured that HCV transmission did not occur If anti-HCV antibody is positive, will need confirmatory HCV RNA testing If HCV RNA is positive, will refer to hepatology/infectious disease for treatment Gastrointestinal Symptoms: Isolated nature of symptoms most consistent with viral gastroenteritis Supportive care with hydration and bland diet Return precautions if symptoms worsen, develop jaundice, dark urine, or right upper quadrant pain Patient Education: Reviewed low risk of HCV transmission from needlestick (approximately 0.2-1.8%) No post-exposure prophylaxis is available for HCV If infection did occur, highly effective direct-acting antiviral treatments are available with cure rates >95% Disposition: Follow-up as needed based on today's test results May discharge from occupational health follow-up if final testing is negative Return to work without restrictions

llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: This is an 18-month-old white male with resolving fever without source, most likely viral illness. The patient presents with a 5-day history of intermittent fever (maximum 102.6F) that has now resolved. He recently completed amoxicillin for sinusitis and is currently teething. Clinical picture is reassuring: well appearance, afebrile today, clear lungs, normal tympanic membranes, no vomiting, diarrhea, or respiratory distress. The discolored nasal secretions in the morning that clear during the day are consistent with resolving upper respiratory infection. The drooling and fussiness are attributable to teething. Teething may cause mild temperature elevation but does not cause true fever >102F, suggesting a concurrent viral illness that is now resolving. PLAN: Observation and Supportive Care No antibiotics indicated at this time Continue cetirizine for allergic rhinitis as needed Antipyretics (acetaminophen or ibuprofen) as needed for fever or teething discomfort Urinalysis and Urine Culture Obtain urinalysis and urine culture to evaluate for urinary tract infection (most common serious bacterial infection in this age group with fever without source) Parental Education and Precautions Return precautions: Bring patient back immediately if fever recurs >102.5F, develops lethargy, poor feeding, respiratory distress, persistent vomiting/diarrhea, or appears ill Teething management: Supportive care with appropriate teething toys, cold washcloths Follow-up Call with urine culture results in 24-48 hours Return to clinic if fever recurs or new symptoms develop Otherwise, routine well-child visit as scheduled
llm_diagnoses: Resolving fever without source, most likely viral illness
llm_dx_summary: An 18-month-old male with a resolving viral illness presenting as fever without source, currently afebrile and well appearing, with symptoms attributable to teething and allergic rhinitis.

llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: This is a 5-year-old male with acute bacterial sinusitis, persistent presentation. The patient was treated with amoxicillin for left acute otitis media with initial improvement, but now presents with recurrent left ear pain and persistent thick, purulent nasal discharge that has never fully resolved. The duration of symptoms (greater than 10 days without improvement) and thick purulent nasal congestion meet criteria for persistent acute bacterial sinusitis per AAP guidelines. Exam findings of distorted TM light reflexes bilaterally without erythema suggest possible serous otitis media or eustachian tube dysfunction secondary to ongoing sinusitis. PLAN: Antibiotic therapy: Amoxicillin-clavulanate 90 mg/kg/day divided BID for 10-14 days. Broader coverage warranted given recent amoxicillin exposure. Symptomatic management: Saline nasal irrigation. Age-appropriate analgesics (ibuprofen or acetaminophen) as needed. Follow-up: Recheck in 3-5 days if symptoms worsen or fail to improve within 72 hours of starting antibiotics. Return sooner if develops high fever, severe headache, facial swelling, or appears more ill. Precautions: Discussed red flags with mother. Family context: Discussed hand hygiene importance given all siblings currently ill.

presentation: HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:,  Patient is a 72-year-old white male complaining of a wooden splinter lodged beneath his left fifth fingernail, sustained at 4 p.m. yesterday.  He attempted to remove it with tweezers at home, but was unsuccessful.  He is requesting we attempt to remove this for him.,The patient believes it has been over 10 years since his last tetanus shot, but states he has been allergic to previous immunizations primarily with "horse serum."  Consequently, he has declined to update his tetanus immunization.,MEDICATIONS: , He is currently on several medications, a list of which is attached to the chart, and was reviewed.  He is not on any blood thinners.,ALLERGIES: , HE IS ALLERGIC ONLY TO TETANUS SERUM.,SOCIAL HISTORY: , Patient is married and is a nonsmoker and lives with his wife.  ,Nursing notes were reviewed with which I agree.,PHYSICAL EXAMINATION,VITAL SIGNS:  Temp and vital signs are all within normal limits.,GENERAL:  The patient is a pleasant elderly white male who is sitting on the stretcher in no acute distress.,EXTREMITIES:  Exam of the left fifth finger shows a 5- to 6-mm splinter lodged beneath the medial aspect of the nail plate.  It does not protrude beyond the end of the nail plate.  There is no active bleeding.  There is no edema or erythema of the digit tip.  Flexion and extension of the DIP joint is intact.  The remainder of the hand is unremarkable.,TREATMENT: , I did attempt to grasp the end of the splinter with splinter forceps, but it is brittle and continues to break off.  In order to better grasp the splinter, will require penetration beneath the nail plate, which the patient cannot tolerate due to pain. llm_plan: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN ASSESSMENT: Subungual foreign body (wooden splinter), left fifth finger - successfully removed. The foreign body was removed in its entirety under digital block anesthesia. No signs of infection. Neurovascular function intact. Tetanus prophylaxis - indicated but declined due to reported allergy to "horse serum." This likely refers to equine tetanus antitoxin no longer in use. Modern vaccines do not contain horse serum. PLAN: Tetanus Prophylaxis: Counseled patient that modern tetanus vaccines (Tdap) do not contain horse serum Patient continues to decline despite counseling Documented informed refusal of recommended tetanus prophylaxis Wound Care: Keep wound clean and dry for 24-48 hours Apply topical bacitracin ointment twice daily and change bandage daily May wash hands gently after 24-48 hours Antibiotic Prophylaxis: No systemic antibiotics prescribed at this time. Complete removal and no signs of infection. Wooden splinters carry higher infection risk but observation is appropriate. Monitoring and Follow-up: Return precautions: increasing pain, redness, swelling, warmth, purulent drainage, fever, red streaking, or lymph node swelling Follow-up in 3-5 days for wound check, or sooner if concerning symptoms If infection develops, initiate antibiotics targeting S. aureus and S. pyogenes Patient Education: Reviewed signs of wound infection Emphasized importance of close monitoring given lack of tetanus prophylaxis Provided written wound care instructions
